title: The Bigger Picture — Daily AI Analysis
description: What today's developments could mean for technology, business and everyday life

sections.title: 1. What AI can do now
paragraphs: Fact: The Verge reports that OpenAI is rolling out answers in ChatGPT that mix text with charts, diagrams, forms and tappable buttons, reaching paying users from 7 October and the free and Go plans on 8 October; the quality and safety claims are OpenAI's own and no outside test is reported {C02-01}. Fact: The Verge reports that Microsoft demonstrated its Autopilot agent finding a user's tax papers on a PC, renaming and zipping them and drafting an email to the accountant, with the abilities due in Copilot over the next couple of months; the evidence so far is one video demo {C02-02}. Fact: Maeil Business Newspaper reports that OpenAI says its Codex and ChatGPT Work agents together had 40 million weekly users, a figure that is OpenAI's own and that the article's other numbers do not match {C02-05}. Fact: The Decoder reports that Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 at prices about 75 percent lower on average than the previous Haiku, while noting that its new tokenizer may use more billed units, so real savings could be smaller {C01-02}. Fact: International Business Times reports that Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive of Meta, said in an essay that Meta will release Muse Spark 1.2, one of its strongest models, as open source {C01-03}. Inference: the model race is also becoming a price and reach race: Anthropic cut the price of its small model, Meta plans to give away one of its strongest, and agents are being given access to a person's files; how many people hand over tasks may soon matter as much as which lab tops a test.

Fact: The Guardian reports that OpenAI released more than 370 new mathematical results on 6 October, and that the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, an independent group of mathematical experts, said it does not endorse testing the hardest problems on companies' private models because people may not be able to check or take responsibility for AI-made proofs; OpenAI has promised to work with the Institute but has not said it will stop {C04-04}. Fact: Nvidia says, in its own blog post, that fine-tuned Nemotron models scored above the gold-medal line at the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, with proofs graded by official judges, and that a coding-olympiad run was unofficial and outside the ranking {C01-11}. Fact: Air Street Press says in its ninth State of AI Report that the leading edge is now a three-way race between Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, citing figures that are the report's own {C04-03}. Fact: Scanx reports, citing a joint announcement by Uber and Baidu, that fully driverless Apollo Go robotaxis now take Uber riders in parts of Dubai, with no fleet size or timetable given {C11-17}. Fact: Reuters reports that the US Department of Transportation granted Aurora and other self-driving truck companies a five-year exemption from the rule that a driver must place warning devices around a stopped truck, and that Aurora runs about 20 trucks on public roads {C11-05}. Inference: capability is running ahead of verification. In mathematics the Institute for Advanced Study is questioning how AI-made proofs are checked; on the road a regulator is clearing the way. Weak signal (our view): in both cases a body outside the companies is now setting the terms.

sections.title: 2. People and society
paragraphs: Fact: Bloomberg reports, as relayed by The Straits Times, that Kevin Sneader, who leads Goldman Sachs' business in Asia-Pacific outside Japan, told the Milken Institute Asia Summit that new hires now oversee AI agents from their first day, and that Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said banks will need fewer fresh graduates for analysis and preparation work; these are conference remarks, not a stated bank plan {C14-03}. Fact: Bloomberg reports, as relayed by The Economic Times, that new graduates in India are finding entry-level jobs at global firms' back-office hubs harder to get as AI takes routine tasks, with Citigroup's net hiring in India down to about 2,000 this year from about 4,000, while the feature finds little evidence yet of mass job losses {C14-04}. Fact: Business Insider reports that Amazon cut roles across several teams on 6 October while preparing to spend a record $220 billion on AI infrastructure; Amazon calls the number small and an unnamed person puts it under 1,000 {C14-01}. Fact: The Guardian reports, after interviews with more than two dozen refugees in Kenya's Kakuma camp, that low-paid online tasks such as transcription and data entry are drying up, with the International Trade Centre estimating that such work has fallen by about 50 percent since 2022 {C14-06}. Fact: The Guardian reports that Co-op Legal Services uses an AI model to score its advisers' calls with customers on more than 50 points, which a whistleblower calls oppressive and the company calls a support tool {C14-05}. Fact: CXOToday reports, citing an essay by Daron Acemoglu, the Nobel laureate and MIT professor, that AI job losses could take at least ten years and affect only about 5 percent of people {C05-14}. Inference: the first people to feel AI at work are at the two ends of the ladder, the graduate who is not hired and the data worker whose task disappears, while the evidence of mass job losses is still thin.

Fact: The Verge reports that Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that reviews apps for youth safety, says ChatGPT for Teens fails to send parents alerts when it should and still does children's homework, and that OpenAI answers that the tests may have run before its parental controls were fully active {C14-02}. Fact: Seoul Economic Daily reports that South Korea's Ministry of Health and Welfare and the Korean Neuropsychiatric Association issued the country's first guidelines on using generative AI for mental-health support, citing a survey in which 68.8 percent of recent AI users had used it for emotional purposes and 14.6 percent had judged themselves to have a mental illness from AI conversations or accepted an AI answer as a diagnosis; the figures are self-reported {C10-11}. Fact: Skin Analytics says in a release that its AI tool will sort skin-cancer referrals across all 18 NHS trusts in south-east England from this autumn, reaching a further 9 million people, with no accuracy figures given {C10-05}. Fact: Hindustan Times reports that India's National Medical Commission, the country's medical regulator, has banned AI-made patient testimonials and faked treatment results in medical advertising, with penalties up to removal from the register {C10-06}. Inference: in the services that touch people most directly, teenagers' chats, mental health and cancer referrals, what arrived today is guidance, company claims and one outside critic's test, not independent accuracy results. Unknown: no entry today reports an independent accuracy figure for any of the health tools it describes.

sections.title: 3. Safety, security and law
paragraphs: Fact: Reuters reports, as carried by The Japan Times, that CrowdStrike, the US security firm, said in a report on 7 October that the attacker behind recent hacks of South Korean banks may be a 26-year-old in China's Guangdong province who used AI tools, while cautioning that it cannot definitively identify the person {C12-02}. Fact: SBS News reports, citing a threat report from the security firm S2W, that hundreds of servers worldwide run the same open-source AI penetration-testing tools used in those hacks, and that leaked loan-inquiry records could fuel targeted voice phishing {C12-05}. Fact: BleepingComputer reports that researchers at Black Lotus Labs, part of the US network company Lumen, say the PoeLLM malware has compromised more than 3,400 servers, many running exposed AI tools, and that the operator is not confidently identified {C12-03}. Fact: Infosecurity Magazine reports, citing the security firm Barracuda, that one phishing campaign hid instructions for AI assistants inside emails so that an assistant summarising an inbox could be told to present the message as legitimate; Barracuda did not say how widespread it was {C12-04}. Fact: GitHub says its local sandbox, which limits the files, network and passwords that Copilot's tools can reach, is now released to all users at no extra cost {C03-03}. Fact: The Register reports that Amazon Web Services released Strands Box, open-source software that runs AI agents inside a sandbox and checks each action against rules, and that Marc Brooker, AWS vice president and distinguished engineer, said developers still have to decide what access an agent gets {C03-04}. Inference: the attack tools are spreading, S2W counts the same open tools on hundreds of servers, and the defence is arriving as sandboxes that only work if someone sets the rules. The bank hacks keep producing new entries because each report adds a piece: a suspect CrowdStrike cannot confirm, the tools, and the leaked data.

Fact: Roll Call reports that Maria Cantwell, the Democratic ranking member of the Senate Commerce Committee, released a six-point framework on 7 October for federal safety testing of the most powerful AI models, with the National Institute of Standards and Technology setting standards; it has no bill text and comes from the minority party {C13-01}. Fact: Axios reports, as relayed by International Business Times, that Senator Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent in the US Senate, wrote to Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, and Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive of Meta, urging a pause in AI development, and that a law forcing one is unlikely to pass in the current Congress {C05-05}. Fact: ABC News reports that Andrew Charlton, Australia's Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy, said in a Sydney speech that AI developers should have to show their safety systems work, under laws modelled on banking and aviation rules, with national standards due by the end of 2026 and laws planned for 2027 {C13-08}. Fact: Moneycontrol reports that Ashwini Vaishnaw, India's Union IT Minister, said the government will publish a consultation paper on AI rules within a month {C13-07}. Fact: The Register reports that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the country's central bank and finance regulator, published its first AI risk guidelines for financial firms, expecting every AI use to be reviewed by people who did not build it before it goes live {C13-12}. Fact: Euronews reports that Denmark is due to introduce a bill banning the sharing of realistic AI deepfakes of a person's face or voice without consent, with Zenia Stampe, Denmark's culture minister, saying the aim is to make tech giants take manipulated content down quickly {C13-11}. Fact: The Associated Press reports that Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, told an audience in Singapore that countries must act faster on debt and AI rules, in a speech ahead of the Fund's Bangkok meetings rather than a new policy {C05-01}. Fact: WIRED reports that the Pentagon's Tradewinds program lets it award AI deals in under a week in some cases on the strength of five-minute company videos, and that Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa warns of weak oversight {C13-03}. Inference: in two days, Australia's minister, Singapore's central bank and a senior US senator moved toward the same idea, show the safety system works before release, while India and Denmark announced rules on other parts of AI; none of these is yet a binding law on safety testing. The dated commitments on safety testing are Australia's end-of-2026 standards and India's paper within a month; on frontier-model safety, everything from Washington is a letter or a framework. Inference: the Pentagon, by contrast, is making its AI purchasing faster.

sections.title: 4. Infrastructure
paragraphs: Fact: Startup Fortune reports that TSMC, the Taiwanese chipmaker, said its third-quarter revenue rose 51 percent from a year earlier, beating the estimate Bloomberg reported, which suggests demand for AI chips has held up for now {C07-02}. Fact: Focus Taiwan reports that the union at Micron's Taoyuan memory-chip plant in Taiwan voted 88.3 percent to authorise a strike over profit-sharing, that no date is set, and that Jerry Lin, chairman of the Taoyuan union, said a surprise strike is among the options after the company's board meets on 8 and 9 October {C08-06}. Fact: Tom's Hardware reports, citing Bloomberg, that Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, said Intel will stay part of Terafab, the chip venture of SpaceX, Tesla and xAI, and that Elon Musk, chief executive of SpaceX, Tesla and xAI, says Terafab will build and run its own plant {C08-04}. Fact: The Washington Post reports, as relayed by Newser, that minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting rank the AI infrastructure boom above tariffs as a key force keeping goods prices high, and that the Fed now expects inflation to stay above its 2 percent goal until 2029 {C09-04}. Inference: the chip supply chain is tight enough that a strike vote at one Taiwan plant is news, and the central bank of the United States now names the build itself as a reason prices stay high. That is a new kind of cost: the AI build is no longer only a bill for its builders.

Fact: Reuters reports, as carried by NBC News, that drones hit a major Yandex data centre in Russia's Ryazan region, causing a fire and suspending operations; the report does not say who launched them {C09-01}. Fact: The Financial Times reports, as relayed by BigGo Finance, that China is building AI data centres fast in its energy-rich inland regions, with 89 built or planned in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, alone {C09-02}. Fact: FOX 7 Austin reports, citing releases from NextEra Energy, the US Department of Commerce and Related Digital, that a 6.47-gigawatt gas plant is planned in Encinal, Texas, to power a 5-gigawatt data centre, with the first stage due in 2029 {C09-10}. Fact: Reuters reports that Sesterce, a French AI infrastructure group, plans a Finnish data-centre site costing more than 10 billion euros, with an unnamed anchor customer {C09-05}. Fact: Bloomberg reports that CoreWeave, the US AI cloud company, will open its first Indian data centres near Mumbai, with the first phase not due until mid-2028 {C09-06}. Fact: WFAE reports that Duke Energy and data-centre operators agreed a special electricity rate for big power users in North Carolina under which new data centres pay upfront for dedicated facilities, subject to state approval {C09-03}. Fact: Data Center Dynamics reports that Denmark's parliament passed an emergency grid plan that puts data centres at the back of the queue; we could read only the headline, and the plan's details and timing are not yet clear {C09-07}. Fact: Fox News reports that the Memphis City Council voted 7 to 5 to delay until 20 October a vote on a 12-month pause on new data centres, at a meeting that turned chaotic {C09-08}. Fact: Politico reports, in a story carried by Business Insider, that National Compute, a new company pooling computing from major tech firms, plans to donate $100 million in computing credits to the US government's Genesis Mission science push, with the announcement expected Thursday, according to two people familiar with the matter {C04-02}. Inference: new building is planned in energy-rich inland China, Finland, south Texas and India, while places that already host data centres, Denmark, North Carolina and possibly Memphis, are writing rules that put them behind households or make them pay their own way. Scenario: if both trends hold, capacity due from 2028 arrives in new regions with new grids, and the drone strike in Ryazan is a reminder that a data centre can be a wartime target.

sections.title: 5. Markets
paragraphs: Fact: Euronews reports Samsung's own estimate of a third-quarter operating profit of about $80 billion, which if confirmed on 29 October would be the biggest quarterly operating profit ever reported by a technology company; it is an estimate, driven by tight supply of memory chips {C07-01}. Fact: Seoul Economic Daily reports, citing ICE Data Services, that the cost of insuring SpaceX's debt against default hit a record as the company seeks about $40 billion to buy Nvidia computing, with the extra interest on its 2036 bonds up to 193 basis points from 140 in June {C07-03}. Fact: The Wall Street Journal reports, citing people familiar with the talks, that Broadcom is working to raise more than $50 billion for a custom chip it is building with OpenAI and that Oracle is in early talks with Apollo and Goldman Sachs to fund a large chip purchase {C06-04}. Fact: Fortune reports that, on estimates by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a researcher at Columbia Business School, the capital spending of Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet will exceed their combined operating cash flow for the first time in 2026 {C07-10}. Fact: Reuters reports that Asian shares fell on Thursday as government bond markets came under strain, partly because major tech companies are reportedly seeking billions in new debt {C07-04}. Fact: Bloomberg reports that Robert Rubin, the former US Treasury secretary and former Goldman Sachs co-chairman, warned of circularity risk, the overlap of commitments between AI suppliers, customers and investors, while still calling the US the best place to invest {C05-06}. Fact: The Associated Press reports that Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, warned that if AI company earnings fall short, heavy borrowing by the biggest cloud companies could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock {C05-01}. Fact: The Japan Times reports that Kentaro Okuda, chief executive of Nomura Holdings, and Akihiko Ogino, chief executive of Daiwa Securities Group, expect Japan's rally to last into 2027 but call a turn against AI the main risk {C07-08}. Fact: Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the deal, that Firmus, the Australian data-centre company, closed its share-sale order book a day early as investors worried the listing could be pulled, with the price unclear {C06-06}. Inference: the same day brought Samsung's estimate of what would be the biggest quarterly operating profit ever reported by a technology company, and a record cost for insuring SpaceX's debt as it seeks $40 billion for Nvidia computing. The money is still flowing to the build, but on one researcher's estimate the five biggest spenders will this year spend more than their businesses earn in cash, and the warning now comes from the IMF, not only from investors. Our view: the cost of that debt is the variable to watch. Markets share of this analysis: section 5 is 9 percent of the words; counting the market material in the forecasts, the watch list and the scenarios as well, about 26 to 29 percent on the second reader's count.

sections.title: Forecasts
paragraphs: 1. TSMC keeps or raises its full-year 2026 outlook when it reports on 15 October. Probability 70 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: medium. Signal: third-quarter revenue up 51 percent and above the estimate Bloomberg reported {C07-02}. Confirms: a raised revenue or spending outlook. Weakens: talk of customers slowing orders, or a flat outlook. Affects: buyers of phones and computers who pay for chips, then the chip supply chain and investors.

2. Samsung's confirmed third-quarter operating profit on 29 October lands within 5 percent of its own estimate. Probability 85 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: medium. Signal: the company's estimate of 107.4 trillion won {C07-01}. Confirms: the published figure. Weakens: a one-off charge or a late fall in memory prices. Affects: workers and suppliers in South Korea's chip industry, then memory buyers and investors.

3. At least one of the three reported private-credit chip financings, Broadcom, Oracle or SpaceX, is signed on roughly the reported size within 3 months. Probability 60 percent. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: low. Signal: the Journal says the Broadcom and Oracle talks are early and could change {C06-04}, and SpaceX's insurance cost is already at a record {C07-03}. Confirms: a signed deal near the reported size. Weakens: a smaller deal, a higher rate, or the gauge on SpaceX's bonds rising further. Affects: the pension and credit funds that lend the money, then Nvidia's and Broadcom's order books.

4. Three scenarios for the AI debt market over 3 months, which add up to 100 percent: (a) the reported deals close at or near their sizes at a modestly higher cost, 55 percent; (b) at least one shrinks or is repriced sharply, 35 percent; (c) one fails outright and other borrowers pull back, 10 percent. Horizon: 1 to 3 months. Confidence: low. Signal: Asian shares falling as bond markets strain {C07-04}, the IMF's warning {C05-01} and the estimate by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a researcher at Columbia Business School, that spending outruns cash this year {C07-10}. Confirms or weakens each: the rate and size of the next deal to close. Affects: savers whose funds hold the bonds and the shares, then the borrowers.

5. Micron's Taoyuan union calls a strike within 4 weeks. Probability 35 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: low. Signal: an 88.3 percent strike mandate, with the union's answer tied to the board's proposals after its 8 to 9 October meeting {C08-06}. Confirms: a strike date or a surprise walkout. Weakens: a revised profit-sharing offer. Affects: the plant's workers, then memory buyers already facing tight supply {C07-01}.

6. The Memphis City Council passes the 12-month pause on new data centres on 20 October. Probability 45 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: low. Signal: the delay passed only 7 to 5, and opponents argue a pause pushes projects to nearby counties {C09-08}. Confirms: a recorded vote for the pause. Weakens: a further delay or a narrower study motion. Affects: Memphis residents worried about power, water and air, then developers.

7. India publishes its AI consultation paper by about 8 November, within the month its minister promised on 8 October. Probability 60 percent. Horizon: days to 4 weeks. Confidence: low. Signal: the minister's own one-month timeline {C13-07}. Confirms: the paper is released. Weakens: silence past the date. Affects: Indian users of AI services and the firms that build them.

8. The US Congress passes a binding law requiring federal safety testing of frontier AI within 12 months. Probability 10 percent. Horizon: 3 to 12 months. Confidence: medium. Signal: a framework with no bill text from the minority party {C13-01}, a senator's letter that is unlikely to become law {C05-05}, and Democratic plans whose content is not yet clear {C13-09}. Confirms: a bill with bipartisan sponsors reaching a committee vote. Weakens: no hearing scheduled by year end. Affects: everyone who uses the largest models, then the labs.

sections.title: A. Highest conviction developments to watch
paragraphs: The dates below come from the day's entries, from the companies and institutions themselves, or from published calendars, and each one says where it comes from. Where a date is not confirmed, it says so.

1. 8 to 9 October: Micron's board meets, and the Taoyuan union says its next step depends on the board's proposals (Focus Taiwan, {C08-06}). Also 8 October: ChatGPT's interactive answers reach free users (The Verge, {C02-01}), Denmark's deepfake bill is due to be introduced (Euronews, {C13-11}), and National Compute's $100 million donation to the Genesis Mission is expected to be announced on Thursday, a date that rests on two unnamed people and is not confirmed (Politico, {C04-02}). Why: the Micron meeting is the first test of whether tight memory supply turns into a labour dispute; the ChatGPT rollout is the day the new answer format reaches free users, with no outside test yet.

2. 10 October: World Mental Health Day, the date South Korea's new guidelines on AI for emotional support were timed for (Seoul Economic Daily, {C10-11}). Why: it is South Korea's first national guidance for people who talk to chatbots about their feelings; what other health ministries say that day shows whether Korea is first or alone.

3. 12 to 18 October: the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, with the plenary scheduled for 16 October, subject to change (source: the IMF's own meetings page). Why: the Singapore speech by Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, was the warm-up (Associated Press, {C05-01}); a change would be the Fund naming AI investment as a risk to growth or to banks in its headline findings at the meetings.

4. 13 October: JPMorgan Chase reports third-quarter results, the first large US bank of the season (source: the company's notice of 17 September 2026). Why: Oracle is reported to be in talks with Goldman Sachs and Apollo to fund chips (Wall Street Journal, {C06-04}) and Robert Rubin, the former US Treasury secretary and former Goldman Sachs co-chairman, warns of circular commitments (Bloomberg, {C05-06}); what the first big bank says about lending to data centres and AI builders is the first measured check from the lenders' side.

5. 14 October: US consumer prices for September, at 8:30 a.m. Eastern (source: published release calendars citing the Bureau of Labor Statistics schedule; we could not open the Bureau's own calendar, so treat the date as very likely rather than confirmed). Why: the Fed's minutes name the AI build as a force keeping goods prices high (Washington Post via Newser, {C09-04}); a hot number raises the cost of every borrowed dollar in section 5, a cool one takes the pressure off.

6. 15 October: TSMC's third-quarter earnings conference, at 2 p.m. Taiwan time, with the company in its quiet period from 5 to 14 October (source: TSMC's investor relations page). Why: it turns the 51 percent revenue rise (Startup Fortune, {C07-02}) into an outlook. A raised 2026 outlook says AI chip demand is still measured in orders; a flat one is the first crack.

7. 20 October: the Memphis City Council's rescheduled vote on a 12-month pause on new data centres (Fox News, {C09-08}). Why: it is the next recorded council vote on whether a city can stop the build, after Denmark's parliament put data centres at the back of its grid queue (Data Center Dynamics, {C09-07}).

8. 27 to 28 October: the US Federal Reserve meets, with the decision at 2 p.m. Eastern on 28 October and no new projections at this meeting (source: the Federal Reserve's October 2026 calendar). Why: the rate is the price of the debt in section 5 and the minutes already discuss AI (Washington Post via Newser, {C09-04}). Late October, dates not confirmed: Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are expected to report quarterly results in the same window, based on past years; none of the day's entries gives a date. Why: their capital spending plans are the one number that tests the estimate by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a researcher at Columbia Business School, that spending outruns cash this year (Fortune, {C07-10}).

9. 29 October: Samsung's full third-quarter results (Euronews, {C07-01}). Why: it confirms or corrects the largest quarterly operating profit a technology company has ever estimated, and shows how much came from memory prices rather than volume.

10. By about 8 November: India's consultation paper on AI rules, on the minister's one-month promise (Moneycontrol, {C13-07}); by the end of 2026: Australia's national AI safety standards, with laws planned for 2027 (ABC News, {C13-08}); 23 November: public comments due to the US Copyright Office on music streaming fraud (Billboard, {C13-14}). Why: among the day's many frameworks and letters, these carry their own dates.

Without a date, but decisive: the price and fate of the Firmus share sale (Bloomberg, {C06-06}); whether the Broadcom and Oracle financings are signed and at what rate (Wall Street Journal, {C06-04}); whether Isomorphic Labs closes a round at $40 billion or more (Bloomberg, {C06-02}); OpenAI's answer to the Institute for Advanced Study on checking its mathematics results (The Guardian, {C04-04}); and the first independent test of Haiku 5.5's real cost per task (The Decoder, {C01-02}).

sections.title: B. Low probability, high impact scenarios
paragraphs: 1. The SpaceX borrowing is cut back or repriced sharply and other AI borrowers follow, close to the risk that Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, warned of (Associated Press, {C05-01}), with the record insurance cost on SpaceX's bonds (Seoul Economic Daily, {C07-03}) and Thursday's bond-market strain (Reuters, {C07-04}) as the early signs. Probability: about 10 percent in 3 months. 2. An AI-assisted bank attack outside South Korea causes losses large enough to force regulators to act, given that the same open tools run on hundreds of servers worldwide (SBS News, {C12-05}) and that CrowdStrike cannot yet definitively identify the attacker behind the Korean hacks (Reuters via The Japan Times, {C12-02}). Probability: under 10 percent in 3 months. 3. A surprise strike at Micron's Taoyuan plant tightens memory supply further, at a time when tight memory supply is already behind Samsung's record estimate (Focus Taiwan, {C08-06}; Euronews, {C07-01}). Probability: about 15 percent in 4 weeks. 4. Data centres outside Russia are attacked physically, after the drone strike on Yandex's Ryazan site (Reuters via NBC News, {C09-01}). Probability: under 5 percent in 3 months. 5. A US regulator or court blocks a major model release on safety grounds before any law passes, a step beyond what the framework of Maria Cantwell, the Democratic ranking member of the Senate Commerce Committee, proposes (Roll Call, {C13-01}). Probability: under 5 percent in 12 months.

sections.title: C. Signals that would change this view
paragraphs: Toward more risk: TSMC guiding flat or lower on 15 October ({C07-02}); the insurance cost on SpaceX's bonds rising past today's record ({C07-03}); the Firmus sale pulled or priced far below what was marketed ({C06-06}); a Micron strike date ({C08-06}); Samsung's confirmed profit well below its estimate ({C07-01}); a second bank sector hit by the tools S2W describes ({C12-05}). Toward less risk: the Broadcom or Oracle deal signed at a rate close to other investment-grade borrowers ({C06-04}); the SpaceX gauge falling back toward its June level ({C07-03}); a cool September inflation print and a Fed statement that no longer names the AI build ({C09-04}); OpenAI agreeing a checking process with the Institute for Advanced Study ({C04-04}); an outside test confirming Haiku 5.5's savings per task ({C01-02}). Toward a different story altogether: India or Australia publishing testing rules with teeth on their stated dates ({C13-07}, {C13-08}), which would move the centre of AI regulation away from Washington.

sections.title: D. Key unknowns and data gaps
paragraphs: Who launched the drones at the Yandex data centre ({C09-01}). The identity of the attacker behind the South Korean bank hacks, which CrowdStrike says it cannot confirm ({C12-02}). The size, rate and timing of the Broadcom and Oracle financings, which the Journal calls early ({C06-04}). The Firmus price, on which Bloomberg and the Australian Financial Review disagree ({C06-06}). Isomorphic's valuation, which rests on people familiar with the talks ({C06-02}). The source of the report that Nvidia is in talks to add $1 billion to Figure AI, which the article does not give ({C11-02}). The true number of Amazon's cuts ({C14-01}). The size of the global stock moves in the Journal's report, which we could read only as a headline ({C07-05}). Whether National Compute's donation is announced as expected ({C04-02}). Whether Haiku 5.5's lower prices survive its new tokenizer in real use ({C01-02}). Whether OpenAI's 40 million weekly agent users is measured the same way as its other figures, which do not match the article's other numbers ({C02-05}). Whether any of the day's health tools has an independent accuracy figure, which no entry reports ({C10-05}, {C10-07}, {C10-08}).
This is analysis of the news, not financial advice or an investment recommendation.
